indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.2.1: Recognize materials as important resources for providing human needs
indicator.objective: Demonstrate understanding that an object is made of one or more materials

skills.description: Recognise that an object can be made of one material or more than one material
Identify the materials that make up a given object
Give examples of objects made of one material and objects made of more than one material
Explain why some objects need to be made of more than one material

misconceptions: Every object is made of only one material.
A computer is made of only plastic.
If an object has different parts, they must all be made of the same material.
Glass and plastic are the same because they can both be clear.

questions.stem: Is a wooden spoon made of one material or more than one material?
questions.explanation: A simple wooden spoon is made of just one material: wood.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all objects are made of many materials.

questions.stem: Is a mobile phone made of one material or more than one material?
hints: Look at the screen and the case.
questions.explanation: A mobile phone is made of more than one material, such as plastic, glass, and metal.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a phone is just one solid block of material.

questions.stem: Which materials are used to make a simple wooden pencil?
hints: What is the dark part inside?
questions.explanation: A pencil is made of wood (the outside) and graphite (the dark writing part inside).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a pencil is only wood.

questions.stem: Which of these objects is made of just one material?
hints: Which one is natural and solid all the way through?
questions.explanation: A stone is made of one material (rock).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think simple objects are made of many materials.

questions.stem: A ruler is made of one material. What is it likely to be?
questions.explanation: Many simple rulers are made of just one material, like plastic or wood.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think rulers have multiple parts.

questions.stem: Kofi has a school bag. It has a main body, a zip, and straps. What materials is it likely made of?
questions.explanation: A school bag is made of multiple materials: cloth for the body, metal for the zip, and sometimes plastic for the straps.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the whole bag is just one material.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of an object made of more than one material?
hints: Are the blades and handles the same material?
questions.explanation: Scissors are made of metal (blades) and plastic or metal (handles).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think scissors are just metal.

questions.stem: What is a glass window made of?
hints: Look at the part that holds it.
questions.explanation: A window is made of glass (the pane) and wood or metal (the frame).
questions.misconception: Pupils may say it is only glass.

questions.stem: Why is a computer made of more than one material (plastic, glass, metal)?
options: Because different parts need different properties
Because it is a big object
Because it is made in a factory
hints: What is the screen made of?
What is the case made of?
questions.explanation: Different materials are used because they have different properties: glass is transparent for the screen, plastic is mouldable for the case, and metal conducts electricity for the wires.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think objects are made of multiple materials just because they look complex.

questions.stem: Ama has a pair of shoes. The top is leather and the bottom is rubber. What are the materials?
questions.explanation: The shoes are made of leather (the top) and rubber (the sole).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think shoes are only one material.

questions.stem: Name one object in your classroom made of more than one material.
hints: Does it have different parts made of different things?
questions.explanation: A chair is often made of wood (seat) and metal (legs).
questions.misconception: Pupils may name an object that is just one material.

questions.stem: Name the two main materials used to make a pencil.
questions.explanation: A pencil is made of wood and graphite.

questions.stem: Why is a car made of metal, glass, rubber, and plastic?
options: Because each material has properties suited for specific parts (e.g., glass for seeing, rubber for tyres)
Because the factory has many materials
Because it is a large object
questions.explanation: Different parts of a car require different properties. Glass is transparent, rubber is strong and flexible, and metal is hard, so multiple materials are needed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think materials are chosen randomly.

questions.stem: Ama says 'All objects are made of only one material.' Is she right?
options: No, some objects like phones and cars are made of more than one material
Yes, all objects are just one material
No, all objects are made of plastic
hints: Think about a pen or a phone.
questions.explanation: Ama is not right. Many objects, especially complex ones, are made of multiple materials.
questions.misconception: Pupils may oversimplify how objects are made.

questions.stem: A bicycle has a metal frame and rubber tyres. Why is rubber better than metal for the tyres?
options: Rubber is bendable and grips the road, while metal would be too hard and slippery
hints: Metal wheels would not be smooth.
questions.explanation: Rubber is better for tyres because it is bendable, providing a smooth ride and good grip, whereas a metal tyre would be hard and slippery.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not think about the function of tyres.

questions.stem: Which of these is made of only one material?
hints: Which one is a simple, single-piece object?
questions.explanation: A simple clay pot is made of just one material (clay).
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all large objects are multi-material.

questions.stem: Choose an object in your home (e.g., a chair, a shoe, a pot) and write down the materials it is made of.

criteria.description: Lists the correct materials it is made of (at least two if applicable)

hints: What are the different parts made of?
questions.explanation: For example, a shoe can be made of leather and rubber.

questions.stem: Explain why a cooking pot needs to be made of metal and not just plastic.

criteria.description: States that metal conducts heat well for cooking
States that plastic would melt or burn on a fire

hints: What happens to plastic on a fire?
How does food cook in a pot?
questions.explanation: Metal conducts heat to cook the food and can withstand high temperatures. Plastic would melt or burn on a stove.

questions.stem: A student says 'A wooden door is made of one material.' Is this completely true?
options: No, it also has metal hinges, screws, and a handle
No, it is made of glass
hints: What is the handle made of?
questions.explanation: A wooden door is mostly wood, but it also includes metal hinges, screws, and often a metal or plastic handle, making it a multi-material object.
questions.misconception: Pupils may overlook the small components that make up an object.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher two materials used to make a car and explain why each is used.

criteria.description: Names two valid materials (e.g., metal, glass, rubber)
Gives a valid reason for each material's use

questions.explanation: Glass is used for windows to see through. Rubber is used for tyres for grip and flexibility.
